script.t: ALCPT Notebook. Readings. The 7 Best Programming Languages to Learn for Beginners. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

Learning how to code opens up many possibilities, from new job opportunities to developing your own applications. However, with so many programming languages available, deciding where to start can be intimidating. The article ranks seven languages for beginners, starting with the easiest and working toward the more challenging ones.

Ruby comes first because its syntax closely resembles spoken English. It is a dynamically typed language, which means that variable types are checked at run-time rather than at compile-time, so it is forgiving for new programmers. Combined with the Rails framework, it powers many database-driven websites, although its performance is less impressive and there are concerns about scalability. Python is another general-purpose language recommended for beginners: you can script basic functionality on your first day. It runs on the backend of Instagram and YouTube, is heavily used by data scientists, and can even build video games with the PyGame library. Its flexibility, however, should not lead to sloppy coding practices.

HTML and CSS are not interchangeable, but they are usually learned together because both are key to web page design. HTML is a markup language that uses tags to define elements, while CSS controls the page layout. HTML5 has also become popular for creating mobile apps. JavaScript, still the world's most popular language, manipulates the output of HTML and CSS and is responsible for on-the-fly updates, interactive features, and animation. It is notably harder to learn, so the author recommends it only once you are comfortable with HTML and CSS.

Java, an object-oriented language, follows the slogan 'write once, run anywhere' and is the main language of Android. It is not as easy, but the web contains a treasure trove of free resources, so you are never alone when you get stuck. Swift was created by Apple for its own platforms as an improvement on Objective-C; its benchmarks are impressive and the Swift Playgrounds app makes learning enjoyable. Finally, R is a free, open-source environment for statistical computing, a favorite for analyzing large data sets in the fast-growing field of big data. Its learning curve may be steep if you are not mathematically inclined. The list is not all-inclusive: your situation may call for C++ or PHP instead.
The seven languages are ordered from easiest (Ruby) to most challenging (R).
Ruby and Python are dynamically typed and forgiving, which makes them ideal starting points.
HTML and CSS should be learned before JavaScript, which is notably more difficult.
Java is the main language for Android, while Swift is Apple's language for iOS and macOS.
R targets statistical computing and big data, but its learning curve can be steep.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. What Is Responsive Web Design?. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

Millions of devices are used worldwide, from phones and tablets to large desktop computers, and users expect to view the same websites on any of them seamlessly. Responsive web design is an approach that ensures a website can be viewed on all screen sizes, regardless of the device. In other words, the website responds to the device and renders its content accordingly: on a mobile phone, for example, the content is resized into a single column.

Although terms such as fluid and flexible were thrown around as early as 2004, the term responsive web design was coined in 2010 by Ethan Marcotte. He believed that websites should be designed for the "ebb and flow of things" rather than remaining static. After he published his article, the term took off and inspired web developers across the globe.

Responsive websites are built to adjust and resize at specific browser widths known as breakpoints. Each breakpoint has a CSS media query that changes the layout once the browser is within a certain range. Put simply, when the width of the browser changes, the code in the background responds and modifies the layout automatically.

Thanks to this flexibility, responsive design is now the gold standard for any website. It offers a seamless on-site experience on every device, and it shows mobile users the most important content first instead of a small snippet. It also makes indexing easier for Google, which improves search engine rank because Google favors mobile-first websites. In the past, developers had to build completely different sites for desktop and mobile; now they update one site, which saves critical amounts of time. Responsive design is also proven to increase conversion rates and to keep page speed equally fast on all devices.

Online shopping illustrates this in the real world. A user may search for a product on a desktop during a lunch break, read reviews on a tablet at home in the evening, and make the final purchase on a mobile phone before turning off the light. Other scenarios, such as planning travel, looking for a new home or looking up recipes, also span a wide range of devices over time, which underlines the importance of a responsive website.
Responsive web design lets a website adapt its layout to any screen size or device.
Ethan Marcotte coined the term in 2010, although words like fluid and flexible were used from 2004.
Sites change layout at breakpoints, which are browser widths controlled by CSS media queries.
Benefits include a better user experience, easier Google indexing, higher conversion rates and time saved for developers.
Everyday tasks such as online shopping often span desktop, tablet and mobile, so responsiveness is essential.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. 6 Best Learn-to-Code Resources Online. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

Learning to code can be useful whether you want to build your own website or make yourself more attractive to potential employers. There is no shortage of options for getting your feet wet in programming, but finding a good entry point can be daunting. The first decision is which language to learn, and the article suggests a simple way to narrow it down: ask yourself what you want to build. Programming languages, like words in English, are a means to an end. If you want a website, HTML, CSS and JavaScript matter. If you want a smartphone app, you must first choose a platform, Android or iOS, and then pick a corresponding language such as Java or Objective-C. A flowchart by Carl Cheo and patient research on Google can also help.

The article then reviews six online resources. Codecademy offers free, fun lessons in basic languages such as HTML and CSS, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, PHP and SQL. Code Avengers adds mini-games after each lesson and focuses on basic concepts rather than the nuts and bolts of a language; it also offers courses in Spanish, Dutch, Portuguese and Russian. Khan Academy suits newbies who already know what they want to build, especially graphics, gaming, drawings and animations, using JavaScript and SQL.

Code School is less beginner-oriented and has a more professional bent, so it is better to arrive after you have a few skills under your belt. It covers mobile languages such as Objective-C and Swift, though full access costs money. Coursera works for self-motivated learners willing to do some digging, because it hosts material on a huge variety of subjects beyond programming. Treehouse requires a paid subscription and is aimed at people who plan to stick with programming professionally or for side projects; its courses are built around objectives, such as building a website.
Finally, for children, the article recommends Blockly, Scratch and Swift Playgrounds, which introduce programming concepts through visuals in engaging, easy-to-follow ways.
Before choosing a language, ask yourself what you want to build.
Websites need HTML, CSS and JavaScript; mobile apps depend on the platform (Android or iOS).
Codecademy, Code Avengers and Khan Academy are the most beginner-friendly options.
Code School and Treehouse have a professional focus and require payment for full access.
Blockly, Scratch and Swift Playgrounds are designed for children.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Why Mathematics Is a Language. A ThoughtCo article on mathematics, condensed for level B2.

Mathematics is often called the language of science. Galileo Galilei wrote that the universe is written in mathematical language, with triangles, circles, and other geometrical figures as its letters, and that without them it is impossible to comprehend a single word. But is mathematics truly a language, like English or Chinese? To answer this, it helps to define language and to see how the vocabulary and grammar of mathematics build sentences.

There are several definitions of language. Linguist Noam Chomsky defined it as a set of sentences constructed from a finite set of elements. Whichever definition is used, a language needs a vocabulary of words or symbols, meaning attached to them, a grammar, a syntax that organizes symbols into propositions, a discourse made of strings of propositions, and a group of people who use and understand the symbols. Mathematics meets all of these requirements, and its symbols and rules are the same throughout the world.

A mathematical equation can be stated in words as a sentence with a noun and a verb. Nouns include numerals, fractions, variables, expressions, diagrams, infinity, and pi. Verbs include equalities, inequalities, and operations such as addition or division. Grammar and syntax are international: formulas are read from left to right, the Latin and Greek alphabets are used for variables and specific concepts, and parentheses and brackets indicate the order in which symbols interact.

Understanding mathematical sentences is a useful teaching tool. Students often find symbols intimidating, so putting an equation into familiar language makes the subject more approachable. Word problems, although disliked, improve comprehension and problem-solving skills. Because math is the same everywhere, it can act as a universal language even when other communication barriers exist.

Not everyone agrees. Some definitions describe language as spoken, while mathematics is written, and complex equations are hard to read aloud. However, this criterion would also disqualify sign language, which most linguists accept as a true language. A strong argument in favor is that modern school curricula use techniques from language education to teach mathematics, since students need robust vocabulary knowledge, fluency with symbols, and comprehension skills.
Galileo described the universe as written in mathematical language.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. How to Overcome Math Anxiety. A ThoughtCo article on mathematics, condensed for level B2.

Math anxiety, or fear of math, is very common. It resembles test anxiety and stage fright: the fear that something will go wrong, that you will forget everything, or that you will be judged poorly. In most cases, math anxiety is the fear of not doing the math right. The mind draws a blank, we expect to fail, and the more frustrated and anxious we become, the more likely we are to go blank again. The pressure of time limits on tests only makes the anxiety grow.

Math anxiety usually stems from unpleasant experiences with mathematics, often the result of poor teaching. Many anxious students show an over-reliance on procedures instead of real understanding. When someone memorizes rules and routines without understanding them, the math is quickly forgotten and panic sets in. A good example is the division of fractions: most people learned to 'invert and multiply' without ever seeing why it works. If math is only a list of memorized procedures, a good memory helps, but a weak memory leads to failure. Understanding is critical, and teachers and parents play an important role in ensuring it.

The article also lists several myths that are simply not true: that you are born with a math gene, that math is only for males, that it is hopeless for average people, that you need a strong logical side of the brain, that some cultures 'never get' math, and that there is only one right way to do math.

To overcome math anxiety, the author recommends keeping a positive attitude, asking questions, and refusing to settle for anything less than understanding. Students should practice regularly, take good notes, and hire a tutor or work with peers when total understanding escapes them. It is not enough to read over notes; you have to actually do the math. Finally, be persistent and do not overemphasize mistakes, because some of the most powerful learning stems from making them.

episodes.title: What Is a Bell Curve in Math and Science?

script.t: ALCPT Notebook. Readings. What Is a Bell Curve in Math and Science?. A ThoughtCo article on mathematics, condensed for level B2.

The term bell curve describes a mathematical concept called normal distribution, also known as Gaussian distribution. The name comes from the shape that appears when you plot the data points of an item that meets the criteria of normal distribution. The center of the curve holds the greatest number of values, so it is the highest point on the arc. This point is called the mean, and in simple terms it is the value that occurs most often, which statisticians call the mode.

The key feature of a normal distribution is that the curve is concentrated in the center and decreases on either side. Because of this, the data is less likely to produce unusually extreme values, called outliers, than other distributions. The curve is also symmetrical, so once you measure the deviation in the data, you can form reasonable expectations about whether an outcome will fall within a range to the left or right of the center. This deviation is expressed in standard deviations.

A bell curve graph depends on two factors: the mean and the standard deviation. The mean sets the position of the center, and the standard deviation determines the height and width of the bell. A large standard deviation creates a short, wide bell, while a small one creates a tall, narrow curve. The total area under the curve equals 1, or 100%. About 68% of the area falls within one standard deviation, about 95% within two, and about 99.7% within three. This is known as the empirical rule or the 68-95-99.7 rule.

A classic example is the roll of two dice. The distribution is centered around the number seven, the most likely outcome at 16.67%, and the probability decreases as you move away from the center. In physics and astronomy, random variations with unknown distributions are often assumed to be normal. This can be a dangerous assumption, but it is a good approximation thanks to the central limit theorem, which states that the mean of any set of variants with a finite mean and variance tends to occur in a normal distribution.

However, some data sets should not be forced to fit a bell curve. Student grades often have two modes, and income, population growth, and mechanical failures also fail to follow the bell-shaped pattern.

script.t: ALCPT Notebook. Readings. How Logical Fallacy Invalidates Any Argument. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

Fallacies are defects that make an argument invalid, unsound, or weak. They fall into two general groups: formal and informal. A formal fallacy can be identified merely by looking at the logical structure of an argument, without reading any specific statement. An informal fallacy, by contrast, can only be detected through an analysis of the actual content of the argument.

Formal fallacies appear only in deductive arguments with identifiable forms. They look reasonable because they mimic valid arguments. For example: all humans are mammals; all cats are mammals; therefore all humans are cats. Both premises are true, but the conclusion is false. If we reduce the argument to its bare structure (All A are C, All B are C, All A are B), it does not matter what A, B, and C stand for: the argument is invalid for the same reason. Stripping away content to examine structure is a useful way to test validity.

Informal fallacies work differently. Consider: geological events produce rock; rock is a type of music; therefore geological events produce music. When we break this down (A = B, B = C, A = C), the structure is valid, so the defect must lie in the content. Here a key term, "rock," is used with two different definitions. Some informal fallacies distract the reader, while others rely on ambiguity to cause confusion.

Aristotle was the first to systematically categorize fallacies, identifying thirteen of them. Since then, many more have been described. One useful classification includes fallacies of grammatical analogy, which resemble valid arguments; fallacies of ambiguity, such as equivocation and quoting out of context; fallacies of relevance, such as ad hominem and appeals to authority or emotion, whose premises are logically irrelevant to the conclusion; fallacies of presumption, such as begging the question and false dilemma, whose premises already assume what they should prove; and fallacies of weak induction, such as ad hoc rationalization and oversimplification, where the link between premises and conclusion is too weak to support it.
A formal fallacy is visible in the structure of an argument; an informal fallacy is visible only in its content.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. What Is an Argument?. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

When people create or critique arguments, it helps to know what an argument is and is not. An argument is not a verbal fight, and it is not the same as making assertions. A Monty Python sketch offers a simple definition: an argument is a connected series of statements intended to establish a definite proposition. Contradiction, by contrast, is just the automatic gainsaying of whatever the other person says. To offer an argument, you must go beyond a claim and give others good reasons to believe it is true rather than false.

Statements such as 'Shakespeare wrote Hamlet' or 'Prostitution is immoral' are assertions, also called propositions. A proposition is the informational content of a statement, and it must be capable of being either true or false. Repeating an assertion, no matter how often, does not constitute an argument. The person making the claim must offer further statements that support it. If the claim is supported, the argument succeeds; if not, it fails. The purpose of an argument is to offer reasons and evidence to establish the truth value of a proposition.

An argument can be broken down into three components: premises, inferences, and a conclusion. Premises are statements of assumed fact that set forth the reasons or evidence for a claim. The conclusion is the claim you finish with. Inferences are the reasoning parts that link the premises to the final conclusion; the conclusion itself is the final inference.

Two kinds of claims appear in arguments. Factual claims purport to offer evidence, and little time is usually spent on them: they are either true or not. Inferential claims express the idea that some fact is related to the sought-after conclusion. Without them, there is no clear connection between premises and conclusion, and sometimes you must ask for the missing links. When you evaluate an argument, you spend most of your time on the inferences: that is where it will stand or fall and where fallacies are committed. Most real arguments are not presented so clearly, but every genuine argument should be capable of being reformulated this way; if it cannot, something is probably wrong.

episodes.title: Status Quo Bias: What It Means and How It Affects Your Behavior

script.t: ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Status Quo Bias: What It Means and How It Affects Your Behavior. A ThoughtCo article on the social sciences, condensed for level B2.

Status quo bias is the tendency to prefer that one's environment and situation remain as they already are. It has its strongest impact on decision-making: when we choose, we favor the familiar option over less familiar alternatives that might be more beneficial. The bias affects every kind of decision, from trivial choices such as which soda to buy to major ones such as selecting a health insurance plan.

The term was coined in 1988 by William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser. In one experiment, participants imagined inheriting a large sum of money and had to choose among fixed investment options. In the neutral version, no option was presented as the current one, and all choices were equally valid. In the status quo version, the money was already invested in a specific way, and one option retained that portfolio. Participants strongly preferred the status quo option, and the more choices they were given, the stronger that preference became.

Psychologists explain the bias through several principles, all of them considered irrational. Loss aversion means people weigh potential losses more heavily than potential gains, so they focus on what they could lose by abandoning the status quo. The sunk cost fallacy leads people to keep investing time, money, or effort in an endeavor simply because they have already invested in it. Cognitive dissonance, the discomfort caused by inconsistent thoughts, pushes people to stick with the current option rather than weigh alternatives. Finally, the mere exposure effect states that people prefer what they have been exposed to before, and by definition we are exposed to the status quo more than to anything else.

Keeping the status quo is not always irrational. When the transition cost of switching is greater than the gains, staying put is a rational choice. The bias becomes irrational only when someone ignores options that would improve their situation just to keep things the same.

Real-world examples are pervasive. Relocated German townspeople chose a layout similar to their old town even though it was inefficient. Consumers rejected New Coke despite preferring it in blind taste tests. Incumbent candidates are more likely to win than challengers, and in a retirement plan only a tiny share of participants changed their investment distribution each year, often without being able to justify it.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. What "Introvert" and "Extrovert" Really Mean. A ThoughtCo article on the social sciences, condensed for level B2.

Imagine your ideal evening. Would you rather go out for dinner with a large group of friends, or spend the night with one close friend and a good book? Psychologists use answers to questions like these to measure introversion and extroversion: personality traits that describe how we prefer to interact with other people.

Today many psychologists place these traits within the five-factor model of personality. According to this theory, a personality can be described by five traits: extroversion (introversion is its opposite), agreeableness (altruism and concern for others), conscientiousness (how organized and responsible someone is), neuroticism (how often someone experiences negative emotions), and openness to experience (imagination and curiosity). Each trait ranges along a spectrum. Extroverts tend to be social, talkative, assertive, and likely to seek out excitement. Introverts tend to be quieter and more reserved. However, shyness is not the same as introversion, and introverts are not antisocial. As the author Susan Cain puts it, they are "differently social": she loves her family and close friends, but she also craves solitude.

In 2011, psychologists at Wellesley College proposed four kinds of introverts. Social introverts enjoy time alone or in small groups. Thinking introverts are introspective and thoughtful. Anxious introverts tend to be shy, sensitive, and self-conscious in social situations. Inhibited or restrained introverts do not seek excitement and prefer relaxed activities.

Is one type better? Research shows that extroverts do experience positive emotions somewhat more often on average. Yet there are also "happy introverts": in one study, about one-third of the happy participants were introverts. Cain points out that American society often treats extroversion as a good thing, for example by encouraging group work in classrooms and offices. In doing so, it neglects what introverts can contribute. Introversion may be linked to creativity, and introverts can be good managers because they give employees freedom and focus on the organization's goals rather than their own success.
In short, neither way of relating to others is better than the other. Each has its own advantages, and understanding our traits helps us study and work with others more effectively.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Whistleblower: Definition and Examples. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

A whistleblower is a person, often an employee, who reveals information about activity inside a private or public organization that is considered illegal, immoral, unsafe, or fraudulent. The U.S. Whistleblower Protection Act of 1989 defines whistleblowing as disclosing information that the employee reasonably believes shows a violation of law, gross mismanagement, a gross waste of funds, an abuse of authority, or a danger to public health or safety. In simpler terms, whistleblowers are informants, and their disclosures have exposed the Watergate cover-up, the accounting fraud at Enron and WorldCom, and the health dangers of nicotine.

The term comes from the 19th century, when police officers blew a whistle to alert the public of crimes in progress. In the 1960s, journalists adopted the single word whistleblower to avoid the negative connotations of words such as informant and snitch. An early example was Ralph Nader, whose 1965 book Unsafe at Any Speed attacked the automobile industry. General Motors retaliated by tapping his phone and hiring prostitutes to discredit him, but Nader won a $425,000 settlement, and Congress passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act in 1966.

Research shows that whistleblowers are usually motivated by integrity and a genuine desire to protect the public, not by monetary awards. Many are unwilling to participate in conduct they believe is wrong, even though speaking out can harm their careers. Social pressures also play a role: people are more likely to come forward when others already know about the wrongdoing.

In the private sector, employees typically report to a supervisor, a lawyer, or the police. In 2021, Frances Haugen disclosed thousands of internal Facebook documents, accusing the company of prioritizing profit over public safety. In the public sector, famous cases include W. Mark Felt, known as Deep Throat, who helped expose Watergate; Daniel Ellsberg, who leaked the Pentagon Papers; and Edward Snowden, who revealed mass surveillance programs and was charged with espionage.

Whistleblowers are seen either as heroic martyrs or as traitors. Even those who halted billion-dollar frauds are routinely demoted, fired, or threatened. In the United States, a patchwork of federal and state laws, such as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, protects employees who call attention to violations or refuse to obey unlawful directions.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. National Security Definition and Examples. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

National security is the ability of a country's government to protect its citizens, economy, and other institutions. For most of the 20th century it was strictly a matter of military power and readiness, but the nuclear age and the Cold War made that definition a thing of the past. Today, U.S. policymakers struggle to balance several "national securities": economic, political, energy, homeland, cyber, human, and environmental security.

The modern environment is complicated by violent non-state actors, such as suicide bombers trained by al Qaeda, Somali pirates, warlords in the Niger Delta, and drug cartels in Mexico. Conventional strategy is ill-equipped to deal with them, so analysts suggest three "spoiler management" strategies: inducements, socialization to change their behavior, and arbitrary measures to weaken them. Peace-building and state-building efforts also try to strengthen state institutions. Scholar Sam C. Sarkesian defined U.S. national security as "the ability of national institutions to prevent adversaries from using force to harm Americans."

The primary goals of U.S. strategy, first stated in 1998, are to protect the lives of Americans, maintain the sovereignty of the country, and provide for its prosperity. The 2021 Interim National Security Strategic Guidance added priorities such as deterring adversaries, mainly China and Russia, and sustaining an open international system underwritten by democratic alliances.

The 9/11 attacks still shape U.S. policy. The War on Terror ushered in laws like the USA Patriot Act, which prioritized security at the expense of some civil liberties, and police departments adopted surplus military equipment, blurring the line between warfare abroad and law enforcement at home. The human toll was enormous for U.S. personnel and, even more, for the people of Afghanistan and Iraq.

National security is distinguished from global security, which involves demands like climate change that no single country can handle alone and which require multinational cooperation through organizations such as the UN and NATO. Governments rely on political, economic, military, and diplomatic tactics. The 2018 National Defense Strategy states that inter-state strategic competition, not terrorism, is now the primary concern. Success must be achieved on two levels: the physical, measured by military capacity, and the psychological, which depends on the people's willingness to support the government's goals.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Push-Pull Factors in Immigration. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

Push-pull factors in immigration are the forces that drive people away from one place and draw them toward another. Push factors are often forceful: they demand that a person or group leave a country, or at least give them strong reasons to move, usually because of a threat of violence or the loss of financial security. Pull factors, in contrast, are the positive aspects of a different country that encourage people to immigrate in search of a better life. Although the two may seem diametrically opposed, both typically come into play when a person or population is considering migrating.

Push factors are detrimental conditions that essentially force people to seek refuge elsewhere. They include a sub-standard level of living, food shortage, land or job scarcity, famine or drought, political or religious persecution, pollution, and natural disasters. Under the worst circumstances, speed of exit matters more than choosing the best destination. Not every push factor obliges a person to leave, but the conditions are often so dire that staying means suffering financially, emotionally, or physically. The Great Potato Famine of the mid-19th century, for example, pushed thousands of Irish families to the United States to avoid starvation.

Refugee populations are among the most affected by push factors. They often face genocide-like conditions in their country of origin, usually because of authoritarian governments or groups hostile to a religious or ethnic minority. Jews leaving Germany during the Nazi era, for instance, were threatened with violent death if they remained.

Pull factors help people determine whether relocating would provide a significant benefit. They attract populations because the new country offers something unavailable at home: freedom from persecution, career opportunities, cheap land, or an abundance of food. Students entering universities or seeking jobs in more developed countries, for example, may receive larger salaries and greater opportunities than in their countries of origin.

For some individuals, push and pull factors work together, especially when the push factors are relatively benign. A young adult who cannot find a lucrative job at home may consider immigrating only if the opportunities elsewhere are significantly better.

script.t: ALCPT Notebook. Readings. The 1932 March of the Veterans Bonus Army. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

In the summer of 1932, more than 17,000 U.S. veterans of World War I marched on Washington, D.C. They demanded immediate cash payment of the service bonuses that Congress had promised them eight years earlier. The press called them the "Bonus Army," but the group named itself the "Bonus Expeditionary Force," echoing the wartime American Expeditionary Forces.

The bonus came from the World War Adjusted Compensation Act of 1924, which gave each qualified veteran a certificate worth 125% of his wartime service credit. The catch was that the certificates could not be redeemed until 1945. President Calvin Coolidge had vetoed the bill, saying that "patriotism, bought and paid for, is not patriotism," but Congress overrode his veto. When the Great Depression began in 1929, most veterans lost their jobs, and by 1932 they could not afford to wait.

The veterans set up makeshift camps around the capital. The largest, nicknamed "Hooverville" as a backhanded tribute to President Herbert Hoover, stood on Anacostia Flats, a swampy bog across the river from the Capitol. With families and supporters, the crowd grew to nearly 45,000. The veterans kept order and built military-style sanitation facilities. In June the House passed a bill to move up the payment date, but the Senate defeated it. The protest march that followed turned violent, and two veterans and two police officers died.

On July 28, Hoover ordered the Secretary of War to clear the camps. Infantry and cavalry under General Douglas MacArthur, backed by six light tanks commanded by Major George S. Patton, charged the veterans with sabers, fixed bayonets and tear gas. Hoover then told the troops to stand down, but MacArthur ignored the order, claiming the marchers wanted to overthrow the government, and launched a second charge. By nightfall, 55 veterans were injured and 135 arrested.

The Army saw the operation as a success, but the press called it "a pitiful spectacle." The political fallout helped Franklin D. Roosevelt defeat Hoover in November. In 1936 Congress overrode Roosevelt's veto and paid the bonuses at once, and the episode contributed to the GI Bill of 1944.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. C (programming language). A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

C is a general-purpose programming language created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs between 1972 and 1973. It began as a successor to the B language, and its first purpose was to build utilities for Unix. Soon after, it was used to re-implement the Unix kernel, which had originally been written in assembly language. In 1973, Version 4 Unix was released with its kernel largely rewritten in C, making Unix one of the first kernels not written in assembly.

By design, C gives programmers fairly direct access to memory and to the features of a typical CPU. That is why it is still used for operating system kernels, device drivers, protocol stacks, and embedded systems, from microcontrollers to supercomputers. Yet the language was also meant to be portable: a standards-compliant program can be compiled for many platforms with few changes to its source code.

C is an imperative, procedural language with a static but weakly enforced type system. All executable code lives inside functions, statements end with semicolons, and blocks are grouped with curly braces. Parameters are passed by value, so passing by reference is done with pointers. Pointers let a program read and modify memory directly, and function pointers make run-time polymorphism possible. C has no dedicated string type; strings are arrays of characters ending in a null character. Complex features such as input/output or string handling are not in the core language but in the standard library. A preprocessor handles macros, file inclusion, and conditional compilation.

For example, in the classic "Hello, world" program, the line #include <stdio.h> tells the preprocessor to insert a header file that declares the printf function. Execution begins in the function main, and printf writes the text to the standard output. The sequence \n is an escape sequence that moves the cursor to the next line.

The language was standardized step by step. The book The C Programming Language (1978), by Kernighan and Ritchie, served for years as an informal specification. ANSI ratified the first official standard in 1989, and ISO adopted it in 1990. Later revisions followed: C99 added inline functions and // comments, C11 added multi-threading and atomic operations, C17 only fixed defects, and C23 was published in October 2024. One trap remains: writing = (assignment) instead of == (equality) in a condition often produces no error message.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. C++. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

C++ is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by the Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup. He began work in 1979 at Bell Labs on "C with Classes", an extension of C, because he wanted a language that was as efficient and flexible as C but also offered high-level features for organizing programs. The name C++ was suggested by Rick Mascitti in 1983 and refers to C's ++ operator, which increments the value of a variable. The first edition of The C++ Programming Language appeared in 1985 and served as the definitive reference until an official standard existed.

C++ supports low-level memory manipulation as well as object-oriented, generic and functional programming. Its design rests on two ideas: a direct mapping of hardware features, inherited mostly from C, and zero-overhead abstractions built on top of them. Stroustrup argues that offering both hardware access and abstraction is the basis of C++, and that doing it efficiently is what distinguishes it from other languages. One guiding principle is that unused features should not slow down the finished program. Because of this, C++ is common in operating systems, video games, servers and performance-critical systems such as telephone switches and space probes.

The language is standardized by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). The first standard, C++98, was published in 1998 and was followed by C++03, C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20 and C++23. Since 2012, a new version has been released every three years. The standard covers both the core language and the standard library, which includes containers, algorithms, strings and input/output. An important influence on the library was the Standard Template Library, proposed in 1994.

C++ is often called a superset of C, but this is not strictly true. Most C code compiles in C++, yet some valid C code is invalid or behaves differently. For example, C allows implicit conversion from void* to other pointer types, while C++ does not, for reasons of type safety. To mix both languages, a function must be declared with C linkage using an extern "C" block. The standards committee also left name mangling and exception handling to each compiler vendor, so object code from different compilers is usually incompatible.

C++ has a weakness: it allows manual memory management, so a programmer can inadvertently introduce bugs such as buffer overflow, which are security risks. In March 2025, Stroustrup called on the language community to defend the language. Initiatives such as the C++ Core Guidelines, led by Stroustrup and Herb Sutter, try to help programmers write safer code by following best practices.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Pointer (computer programming). A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

In computer science, a pointer is an object that stores a memory address. That address may belong to another value in memory or, in some cases, to memory-mapped hardware. Obtaining the value stored at that location is called dereferencing the pointer. A useful analogy is a page number in a book's index: flipping to that page and reading it is the equivalent of dereferencing.

Pointers are a very thin abstraction on top of the addressing capabilities of modern architectures. Each unit of memory has a numeric address, so memory works like one very large array. Pointers improve performance in repetitive operations, such as traversing strings, lookup tables, linked lists and trees, because copying a pointer is much cheaper than copying the data it points to. They are also used to pass parameters by reference, to return several values from a function, and to hold the entry points of subroutines.

In C, a pointer is declared with an asterisk, for example int *ptr. The & operator retrieves a variable's address, and the asterisk dereferences the pointer. Suppose a is at address 0x8130 and ptr holds that address. Writing *ptr = 8 makes the computer read the address stored in ptr and put 8 in that location, so a now equals 8. Array indexing is defined through pointer arithmetic: a[i] is equivalent to *(a + i). Adding 1 to a pointer moves it by the size of the type, so on a machine with 4-byte integers, a + 1 advances 4 bytes.

Pointers also allow dynamic memory allocation. The function malloc() reserves a block on the heap and returns a pointer to it, or a null pointer if the allocation fails, and free() returns the block. If a program forgets to free memory it no longer needs, a memory leak occurs. On some microcontrollers, a pointer can be set to a fixed hexadecimal address to control memory-mapped devices directly.

Pointers carry risks. An uninitialized wild pointer may point to an invalid address and cause a segmentation fault. A dangling pointer refers to memory that has already been deallocated and may have been overwritten by unrelated code. Dereferencing a null pointer produces undefined behavior. To reduce these hazards, languages such as Java use opaque references that cannot be manipulated as numbers, garbage collection frees memory automatically, and C++ offers smart pointers based on reference counting. Rust uses a borrow checker to eliminate pointer bugs without garbage collection.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Compiler. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

A compiler is software that translates code written in one programming language, the source language, into another, the target language. The term usually refers to programs that turn a high-level language into a low-level one, such as assembly or machine code, to create an executable program. There are many kinds: a cross-compiler produces code for a different CPU or operating system than the one it runs on, and a bootstrap compiler is a temporary tool used to build a better, more permanent compiler.

An interpreter does a similar job by a different mechanism: it executes code without converting it to machine code, or it runs an intermediate form such as bytecode. Code compiled to native form generally runs faster than interpreted code, while just-in-time compilation offers native speed at the cost of a one-time startup delay. Low-level languages like C are typically compiled, especially when speed matters, because their source maps closely to machine code and gives programmers more control over hardware.

Compilers began in the 1950s. Grace Hopper's team wrote the A-0 compiler in 1952 and coined the term, and John Backus's team at IBM completed the FORTRAN compiler in 1957. Early computers had so little memory that the work had to be split into several small programs, which led to the idea of separate front end and back end stages. Later, Bell Labs developed B and then C, and the Unix kernel was rewritten in C by 1973.

Modern compilers are usually organized in three stages. The front end reads the source, checks syntax and semantics, reports errors, and builds an intermediate representation (IR). To do this it performs lexical analysis, which breaks the text into tokens, then parsing, which builds a tree according to the grammar, and finally semantic analysis, which checks things like types and fills the symbol table.

The middle end optimizes the IR independently of the CPU. Typical optimizations include dead-code elimination, constant propagation and moving computation out of a loop. The back end then generates code for a specific processor, performing register allocation and instruction scheduling. This design lets tools such as GCC and Clang combine several languages with several processors while sharing the same optimizations.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Finite-state machine. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

A finite-state machine (FSM) is a mathematical model of computation. It is an abstract machine that can be in exactly one of a finite number of states at any given time. It changes from one state to another in response to inputs, and each change is called a transition. An FSM is defined by its list of states, its initial state, and the inputs that trigger each transition. Because its memory is limited by the number of states, it has less computational power than a Turing machine.

Many everyday devices behave like state machines. A vending machine dispenses a product when the right coins are deposited, an elevator decides its stops from the floors requested, and a combination lock requires numbers in the proper order. A coin-operated turnstile is the classic example. It has two states, Locked and Unlocked, and two inputs, coin and push. In the Locked state, pushing has no effect; inserting a coin moves it to Unlocked. In the Unlocked state, extra coins change nothing; a push lets one customer through and resets the state to Locked.

A machine can be shown in a state-transition table or in a state diagram. In the diagram, each state is a node, each arrow is a transition labeled with its input, and a circular arrow marks an input that causes no change. Some models also attach an entry action, performed when entering a state, or an exit action, performed when leaving it.

FSMs are classified by what they do. Acceptors give a binary answer: after reading all the input, they accept it if they end in an accepting state and reject it otherwise. The sets of sequences they accept are called regular languages. Transducers produce output. In a Moore machine the output depends only on the current state, which simplifies behavior. In a Mealy machine the output depends on both state and input, which often reduces the number of states.

A machine is deterministic if every state has exactly one transition for each possible input. In a non-deterministic machine, an input may lead to one, several, or no transitions. Any non-deterministic machine can be converted into an equivalent deterministic one, although the result is usually more complex. In practice, FSMs are built with logic gates, flip-flops, or relays, and with a register that stores the current state. They are also used in compilers, where a lexical analyzer turns characters into tokens for the parser.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. UML state machine. A ThoughtCo article on technology and computing, condensed for level B2.

A UML state machine, formerly called a UML statechart, extends the mathematical idea of a finite automaton. It organizes how a device or program works so that it is always in exactly one of several possible states, with well-defined conditional transitions between them. It is an object-based variant of the Harel statechart, and it combines features of Mealy machines (actions that depend on both state and triggering event) and Moore machines (entry and exit actions tied to states).

Many software systems are event-driven: they wait for an event, such as a key press or a data packet, react to it, and then wait again. The reaction depends on the type of event and on the internal state. In UML, an event is a type of occurrence, and each concrete occurrence is an instance. A state machine follows the run-to-completion model: it finishes processing one event before starting the next, and new events wait in a queue. This avoids internal concurrency problems, although the machine's responsiveness is set by its longest step.

Traditional finite-state machines suffer from state explosion. UML solves part of this with extended state: the state variable captures the qualitative aspect, while other variables capture the quantitative aspects. For example, a key_count variable can limit keystrokes to 1000 without creating 1000 states. Guard conditions, which are Boolean expressions in square brackets, enable a transition only when they evaluate to TRUE. Guards should have no side effects, because UML does not define the order in which they are evaluated.

The most important innovation is hierarchically nested states. If a system is in a substate, it is also in the surrounding superstate. When the substate does not handle an event, the superstate handles it instead of discarding it. In a pocket calculator, for instance, the Clear and Off transitions are defined once in the "on" superstate. Orthogonal regions also let a composite state contain independent parts, such as the main keypad and the numeric keypad. Modeling them separately needs 2 + 2 states instead of the 2 × 2 = 4 of a Cartesian product.

Entry and exit actions guarantee initialization and cleanup, much like constructors and destructors. In a toaster oven, the exit action of "heating" disables the heater, so it is off whatever path leads out of that state. Entry actions run from the outermost state inward, and exit actions run in reverse. An internal transition runs actions without changing state and without triggering entry or exit actions, unlike a self-transition.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Spacecraft attitude determination and control. A ThoughtCo article on general knowledge, condensed for level B2.

Spacecraft attitude control is the process of managing the orientation of a satellite or vehicle relative to a reference, such as the stars or the Earth. It matters because antennas must point accurately at Earth, instruments must aim at their targets, solar panels must face the Sun, and short engine burns must be fired in the right direction. Before attitude can be controlled, it must be determined with sensors. The whole system is usually called the attitude determination and control system (ADCS).

Attitude can be described with rotation matrices, quaternions or Euler angles. Euler angles are easy to visualize but suffer from gimbal lock. A rotation matrix needs nine values, while a quaternion needs only four and avoids gimbal lock, so it is a good compromise.

There are two main ways to stabilize a spacecraft. In spin stabilization, the whole craft rotates and its gyroscopic action keeps it steady; Pioneer 10 and 11 used this. In three-axis stabilization, the craft is held fixed in one orientation. This can be done with small thrusters that nudge it back and forth within a deadband of allowed error, as on the Voyager probes, or with reaction wheels. To turn the vehicle on one axis, the wheel on that axis is accelerated in the opposite direction. External torques slowly build up excess momentum, so the wheels must be desaturated with thrusters or, on the Hubble Space Telescope, magnetic torquers. Other actuators include control moment gyros, solar sails and gravity-gradient stabilization, which needs no fuel.

Control algorithms are software that turn sensor data into actuator commands. Most use error signals, the difference between measured and desired attitude, and a simple PID controller satisfies most needs. After release from the launch vehicle, a satellite in low Earth orbit is usually tumbling, so a B-Dot controller detumbles it using magnetic coils that react to changes in Earth's magnetic field. Afterwards the system switches between modes such as safe mode, Sun pointing and nadir pointing.

Determination uses relative sensors, such as gyroscopes, and absolute sensors, such as horizon sensors, Sun sensors, star trackers and magnetometers. Because no single measurement gives the attitude directly, it must be estimated. The most common method is the Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter, which combines previous estimates with new measurements to obtain an optimal result.

A reaction wheel (RW) is an electric motor attached to a flywheel. When the wheel's rotation speed changes, the spacecraft turns in the opposite direction, because angular momentum is conserved. The wheel can only spin around its center of mass, so it cannot move a spacecraft from one place to another.

Spacecraft use reaction wheels mainly for fine attitude control on three axes, and also for fast detumbling. They need no rockets or external sources of torque, which reduces the fuel a mission must carry. They give high pointing accuracy, so they are ideal for tiny rotations, such as keeping a telescope aimed at a star. Because the wheel is a small fraction of the spacecraft's mass, a small, easily controlled change in its speed produces only a small change in angle. Some satellites, such as SCISAT-1, run a wheel at near-constant speed to store a large amount of angular momentum. This "momentum-bias" approach stabilizes an axis in a nearly fixed direction and allows a simpler control system.

For three-axis control, wheels must be mounted along at least three directions. Extra wheels add redundancy, for example four wheels along tetrahedral axes or one spare. A computer controls speed changes electronically. The strength of the wheel's materials sets the speed at which it would come apart, and therefore how much momentum it can store.

Over time, a wheel may accumulate more momentum than its maximum speed allows, which is called saturation. Slowing the wheel down creates an unwanted torque, so designers add other systems to cancel it. Traditionally, small chemical rockets fire during desaturation. More fuel-efficient options exist, such as magnetorquers, which transfer momentum to the Earth through its magnetic field using only electrical power, although they work only where that field is strong enough, as in low Earth orbit. Elsewhere, ion thrusters are the next best choice.

Failures can be serious. If wheels fail, a spacecraft may lose its attitude control and the mission may fail. Kepler lost two of its four wheels between 2012 and 2013 and could no longer point precisely enough for its original planet search, so it moved to a new mission called K2. Hayabusa and Dawn also suffered wheel problems and relied on thrusters. Hubble was designed with four redundant wheels and kept its pointing ability as long as three worked. A related device, the control moment gyroscope, produces larger torques and is used on Skylab, Mir and the International Space Station.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Star tracker. A ThoughtCo article on general knowledge, condensed for level B2.

A star tracker is an optical device that measures the positions of stars using photocells or a camera. Astronomers have measured the positions of many stars with great accuracy, so a satellite or spacecraft can use a star tracker to determine its orientation, also called its attitude. To do this, the device must capture an image of the stars, measure their apparent position in the spacecraft's reference frame, and identify them so that their position can be compared with the known absolute position in a star catalog. A processor may identify the stars by matching the observed pattern with the known pattern of stars in the sky.

In the 1950s and early 1960s, star trackers were an important part of early long-range ballistic and cruise missiles, because inertial navigation systems (INS) were not accurate enough for intercontinental ranges. Before launch, engineers calculated the angle of a chosen bright star for each moment of the flight. This signal was pre-recorded on magnetic tape, which was used to roughly point a telescope at the expected position of the star. At the telescope's focus, a photocell and a spinning disk called a chopper made the star's image appear and disappear repeatedly, producing a signal. Comparing its phase with the chopper's phase gave the angle to the star, and the difference from the expected angle produced an error signal that brought the missile back onto its trajectory.

Star trackers were often combined with an INS, which measures accelerations and integrates them over time to obtain velocity and position. Even tiny errors add up to an appreciable error known as drift. For example, the N-1 system of the SM-64 Navaho missile drifted about 1 nautical mile per hour, so after two hours it was 2 nautical miles off, well outside the desired accuracy of half a mile. In these stellar inertial systems, the INS points the tracker, and the tracker's measurement corrects the accumulated drift. They were especially common from the 1950s through the 1980s.

Today many models are available, including open projects for the CubeSat community. Star trackers need high sensitivity, so they can be confused by sunlight reflected from the spacecraft or by exhaust plumes from its thrusters. They are also prone to optical errors, such as spherical and chromatic aberration, and the identification algorithm can be misled by planets, comets, supernovae, nearby satellites or city light pollution.

About 57 bright navigational stars are in common use, but complex missions rely on whole star field databases. A high-fidelity catalog starts from a standard base, such as the one from the United States Naval Observatory, and is filtered to remove unreliable stars. It may be stored on board or processed at a ground station and uploaded. Star trackers can also help detect space debris and identify satellites.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Silk Road. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. It stretched over 6,400 km on land and linked the Eastern and Western worlds economically, culturally, politically and religiously. The name was coined in the late 19th century and popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen. Some historians prefer "Silk Routes", because the system was an intricate web of land and sea routes, not a single road. Others argue that the classic idea overlooks steppe nomads, India and Iran.

The network began to take shape when China's Han dynasty expanded into Central Asia. Around 130 BCE, the envoy Zhang Qian explored the region, and his reports showed the economic reasons for pushing westward. The Chinese extended the Great Wall to protect the trade route, and the Han army regularly policed it against nomadic bandits. The Parthian Empire served as a vital bridge to the Mediterranean, while Rome became the western terminus. Chinese silk was in great demand there, although many Romans wrongly believed it grew on trees. The Senate issued several edicts against wearing silk, on economic and moral grounds, but in vain.

The system was highly decentralized and security was sparse. Travelers faced banditry, raids and inhospitable terrain, so few people traveled the whole length. Instead, goods passed through a succession of middlemen in a kind of "relay trade". Beyond silk, caravans carried tea, dyes, perfumes, porcelain, horses, camels, honey, wine and gold. Ideas, especially Buddhist and scientific thought, also spread, and so did diseases such as plague, possibly contributing to the Black Death.

There were several routes. The northern route started at Chang'an and split around the Taklamakan Desert, while the southern route crossed the Karakoram mountains, where the Karakoram Highway runs today. A maritime route, run by Austronesian, Persian, Arab and Tamil sailors, connected Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa. Ships carried far larger cargoes and could avoid political conflict, although they faced weather and piracy.

Critics such as Warwick Ball call the Silk Road a "myth" of modern academia. He argues that maritime spice trade with India mattered more to Rome, and that free movement of goods did not exist until the Mongol Empire. From 1453, the Ottoman Empire competed for control of the overland routes, which pushed Europeans to seek alternatives and marked the start of the Age of Discovery. Today, "New Silk Road" describes projects such as China's Belt and Road Initiative, and UNESCO has designated some corridors as World Heritage Sites.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Printing press. A ThoughtCo article on the humanities, condensed for level B2.

A printing press is a machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto paper, cloth, or a similar surface. It improved on older methods, in which paper was rubbed by hand over inked material. The German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg invented it around 1440, and its spread revolutionized literary production and communication in early modern Europe.

Gutenberg combined four existing technologies: the screw press, movable type, the codex book format, and mechanized paper production. He added his own innovations, such as a hand mold for casting type and an oil-based ink suited to metal type. He was also the first to make type from an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony, which was particularly durable. Movable type had appeared earlier in East Asia, but thousands of logographic characters made it costly there, while the Latin alphabet needed only a small set.

To operate a classical press, a compositor set individual metal letters into lines, placed them in a frame called a forme, and inked them with leather ink balls. A sheet of dampened paper, held by the tympan and the frisket, was folded over the type. The compositor then pulled a long lever, the bar, which drove a screw that pressed the platen onto the paper. Around 1800, Lord Stanhope built an iron press that printed a whole sheet in one pull. Later, steam power and rotary motion, introduced by Friedrich Koenig and Richard M. Hoe, allowed millions of impressions per day.

Printing spread quickly: by the end of the 15th century, around 270 European cities had presses, and by 1500 they had produced over 20 million copies. Because the equipment was portable, printers could relocate when authorities tried to curtail them, which made censorship difficult. Printing helped to spread the Reformation, lowered the cost of texts, raised adult literacy, and encouraged books in vernacular languages instead of Latin.

It also changed how people worked and read. Identical copies allowed precise citation and gave authors greater importance, while reading shifted from communal recitation to silent, private reading. Scientists could share discoveries faster and across greater distances. Governments used print for propaganda, and both church and state tried to control it. Some contemporaries criticized it, arguing that printers valued profit over accuracy. Later, offset printing and digital methods replaced the letterpress in commercial work.

The Renaissance, meaning "rebirth", was a European period and cultural movement at the end of the Late Middle Ages and the start of the early modern era. It is usually placed in the 15th and 16th centuries, although some define it more broadly, from the 14th century to the 17th. Its defining feature was the rediscovery and revival of the literary, philosophical and artistic achievements of classical antiquity. It began in Florence, then spread across Italy and the rest of Europe.

Its intellectual basis was humanism, which rested on Roman humanitas and on classical Greek philosophy. Humanism was less a philosophy than a method of learning: scholars studied ancient texts in their original languages and judged them through reasoning and empirical evidence. In the 14th century, scholars such as Petrarch scoured European libraries for Latin works. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, Greek scholars brought precious manuscripts to the West, and the Greek phase of humanism followed. Renaissance scholars differed from earlier medieval ones because they focused on literary and historical texts, not only on science and mathematics.

Historians disagree about why the movement began in Italy. Italy was divided into rich, urbanized city-states, such as Florence and Venice, where merchants brought new ideas from distant lands. Their relative political freedom helped academic and artistic progress, and their wealth paid for large artistic projects. The Medici, a banking family, acted as patrons of artists like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo. Some theorists also suggest that the Black Death, which killed about a third of England's population, changed how people saw life on Earth and raised the value of working people.

The period brought change in many fields. Painters such as Masaccio developed linear perspective and studied light, shadow and anatomy in order to portray the human form realistically. Brunelleschi studied ancient buildings and designed the dome of Florence Cathedral. Machiavelli tried to describe political life as it really was. Writers increasingly used vernacular languages, and the movable type printing press, which appeared in Germany around 1440, made books available to many more people. By the end of the 15th century, it had produced more than 20 million volumes. Historians still debate whether the Renaissance was a true break with the Middle Ages or an extension of it.

Jazz is a music genre that originated in the African-American communities of New Orleans in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It grew out of blues, ragtime, European harmony, African rhythmic rituals, spirituals, hymns, marches and dance music. Its main features are swing and blue notes, complex chords, call-and-response vocals, polyrhythms and, above all, improvisation.

Jazz is hard to define because it covers more than a hundred years of music, from ragtime to rock-influenced fusion. The word itself probably comes from a slang term, "jasm", meaning energy or pep. Its earliest written record dates from 1912, when a baseball pitcher described a "jazz ball" that wobbles unpredictably. Critics have offered broad definitions, and Duke Ellington summed it up by saying, "It's all music."

Unlike classical music, where the performer aims to play the composition as written, jazz values interaction and collaboration. A performer never plays the same tune twice, changing melodies, harmonies and time signatures according to mood and the reaction of the band or audience. In many styles a soloist is supported by a rhythm section of piano or guitar, double bass and drums. In free jazz, even chords, scales and meters may be abandoned.

Its African roots survived partly through call-and-response patterns and body rhythms such as stomping and clapping, because the Black Codes outlawed drumming by enslaved people. The Afro-Cuban tresillo rhythm, which reached New Orleans through the habanera, became a fundamental figure; Jelly Roll Morton called it the "Spanish tinge". Ragtime, led by Scott Joplin, and the blues, which W. C. Handy published as sheet music, also shaped early jazz.

Jazz then evolved through many styles: swing big bands in the 1930s, bebop in the 1940s, cool jazz, hard bop, modal and free jazz, and finally fusion and smooth jazz. Throughout its history, race, gender and religion influenced who played it. Women worked as bandleaders and instrumentalists, and Jewish Americans and mixed bands such as Benny Goodman's helped bring jazz into popular culture.

ALCPT Notebook. Readings. Ancient Olympic Games. A ThoughtCo article on general knowledge, condensed for level B2.

The ancient Olympic Games were a series of athletic competitions among representatives of Greek city-states, held at the sanctuary of Olympia in honor of Zeus. Traditionally dated to 776 BC, they took place every four years, a period called an Olympiad, which became a unit of time in ancient chronologies. The last recorded celebration was in AD 393 under Theodosius I, although archaeological evidence suggests that some games were held afterward.

The Greeks gave the games a mythological origin. One story says Heracles and his brothers raced at Olympia to entertain the newborn Zeus. Another tells how Pelops won a chariot race against King Oenomaus by persuading the king's charioteer to replace the bronze axle pins with wax ones. Historians agree that the games probably date from the eighth century BC, but the exact date of 776 BC cannot be verified. For its first 200 years the event had only regional importance, and Peloponnesian athletes dominated it.

The games were both a religious festival and a political stage. During an Olympic truce, or ekecheiria, athletes and pilgrims could travel safely, although the truce did not stop all wars. City-states used the games to assert dominance, announce alliances and promote themselves, and successful athletes were linked to the spread of Greek colonies. Poets, sculptors and other artists came to show their work to would-be patrons. The statue of Zeus by Pheidias, made of gold and ivory, was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world.

Only freeborn Greek men could compete, although women could take part as owners of chariot horses. The program grew from a single foot race, the stadion of about 190 metres, to as many as twenty events, including running, wrestling, boxing, the pankration and the hoplite race in full armour. Athletes competed naked for most of the games' history, a custom the Greeks felt set them apart from non-Greeks. Winners were rewarded with olive wreaths and honored in victory songs.

Under Roman rule the games declined at first, and Sulla robbed Olympia to finance a war. They revived under Augustus and again in the second century, but Nero damaged their reputation by ordering that his own victories be recognized, even after he fell from his chariot. From the third century the games lost popularity, and flooding, earthquakes and invasions damaged the site before they finally came to an end.

Coffee has a history of many centuries. Wild coffee plants originated in Ethiopia, but the beverage itself has its roots in Yemen, where it was harvested, roasted and brewed. In the 15th century, Sufi Muslims used it to stay alert during their nighttime prayers. There is no confirmed evidence of coffee being drunk as a beverage before that century, so the drink appears to be a relatively recent development.

From Yemen, coffee spread to Mecca and the Arabian Peninsula, and by the early 16th century it had reached Cairo, Damascus and Istanbul. Its permissibility was debated: in 1511 conservative imams banned it at a theological court in Mecca, but the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I overturned the ban in 1524. Despite these disputes, coffeehouses soon became central to urban social life, acting as places for conversation, poetry and political discussion.

Coffee entered Europe in the mid-16th century through Mediterranean trade, especially via Venice. The first mainland European coffeehouse opened in Venice in 1645, and by the late 17th century coffeehouses existed in Holland, England and Germany. In England, they became gathering places for serious religious and political talk, which was so common, and potentially subversive, that Charles II tried to crush them in the 1670s. According to a legend, Pope Clement VIII blessed the drink after trying it, although the story may not be true.

Until the end of the 17th century, the Yemeni port of Mocha was the world's only gateway for coffee. As demand grew, cultivation spread. In 1720, Gabriel de Clieu brought seedlings to Martinique, and from there coffee reached other Caribbean islands and Mexico. By 1788, Saint-Domingue supplied half of the world's coffee. Brazil became the largest producer in 1852 and has held that position ever since. More recently, Colombia, Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Vietnam have emerged as major producers.

The origins of coffee are also surrounded by legends. The best known tells of a goatherder named Kaldi who noticed his goats becoming energetic after eating red berries. However, this story does not appear before 1671, so it is probably apocryphal. Modern genetic research, published in 2020, confirmed that most Arabica plants in the world descend from varieties cultivated in Yemen.
